title: Currently running on Broadway via Second Stage through June 14th! #br...
transcript: This cast of TV, film, and Broadway stars have come together for a wild ride of a play, at the center of which is an ill-fated blind date that we never actually see take place. This is a revival of Gina Gionfriddo's Pulitzer-finalist play, Becky Shaw An acerbic comedy, with a rock solid cast including Alden Ehrenreich from Weapons and Solo Tony winner Lauren Patten, Patrick Ball from the Pitt and Madeline Brewer from The Handmaid's Tale in the slippery title role of Becky Shaw. The events of this play stir up an incredibly knotted web of emotional baggage  among the characters. It's like family drama meets dark romantic comedy. And the lines between those get even more blurry than you might think. Together, it makes this fascinating portrait of characters relying on each other and attaching to each other in deeply unhealthy ways. Like, where's the line between needing someone and loving someone? And how do you know the difference when you're so messed up by your circumstance? I described this play to my friend as like watching a bunch of rats with their tails tied together, just clambering over each other, trying to figure out where they end and the other rats begin. One of the only things I knew about this play beforehand is that the characters were supposedly very unlikeable, and that's not untrue. But there's such an insightful examination of why they are the way they are that I couldn't help but sympathize with them anyway. It also helps that the production is very well acted. Each of them has to walk this extremely tricky line, and they pull it off. It did take me a while to warm up to the play, partly because we're getting to know these characters who, again, don't come off especially well at first. But also the first 25 minutes or so feel like a completely different play and one that I didn't particularly like as much. So it's tempting to say that those first 25 minutes should have just been cut and converted to exposition. But I don't know. I think, in retrospect, the events of the second act wouldn't have the same impact if she had. She's laying the groundwork for what becomes an emotional roller coaster that is funny and devastating at the same time, and largely for the same reasons.
